title: Trump Administration Launches AI Portal for 29,000 Government Websites
summary:
Lead engineer Edward Coristine is building a centralized digital interface to allow US citizens to apply for their first passports from home instead of visiting a postal branch. The new system will let users upload and preview passport photos online and complete the entire application process without leaving the site, expanding current capabilities that only allow for digital renewals.

The project, Americadotgov, launched Sept. 29 as an AI powered single point of entry for information currently spread across 29,000 federal websites. Coristine, a 20 year old who previously worked at Neuralink and the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), is partnering with the National Design Studio to consolidate services such as Medicare and Social Security into the unified portal.

selectedTweets.text:
20 year-old phenom Edward Coristine, the former DOGE engineer better known as "Big Balls," is back in the house and helping the Trump administration to save America and make the the federal government work more efficiently for the American people.

Coristine is now helping build the Trump administration’s new digital front door to the federal government — an effort aimed at giving Americans one place to navigate information and, eventually, complete services now spread across thousands of government websites.

"I think that the fact that there’s 29,000 government websites is pretty insane," Coristine told Fox News Digital in a sit-down interview. "And it is the citizens’ objective to have to go figure out which government website they’re supposed to use for each specific thing."

Coristine — better known around Washington by his attention-grabbing "Big Balls" nickname — sat down with Fox News Digital at the White House to talk about his new role helping build Americadotgov, what he learned during his time at DOGE, the administration’s plans to make more government services fully digital, his experience being attacked in Washington, and how the nickname that helped make him famous actually came from his dad.

Coristine is now working with the National Design Studio on the administration’s revamped Americadotgov, which launched Sept. 29 as an AI-powered single point of entry for information drawn from thousands of government websites. 

President Trump singled out Coristine during the launch, identifying him as the project’s lead engineer and thanking him for his work.

Coristine said his time at DOGE gave him a firsthand look at the frustration Americans face when trying to navigate federal services and helped shape what he is working on now.

"I think we got a lot of feedback that the American government is hard to interact with because you have to navigate the maze of bureaucratic services," Coristine said.

The software engineer had already worked in Musk’s orbit before joining DOGE, spending several months at Neuralink, Musk’s brain-computer interface company, before later joining the government efficiency effort at 19.

"What I think is really special about Americadotgov is it presents a single point of entry to find all the information that you need," he added, including finding government services tailored to the user and asking questions with answers sourced from the federal government.

Coristine pointed to Medicare as one example, saying Americans currently may have to move between Medicaredotgov and the Social Security website to enroll in benefits.

"Companies, generally speaking, only have one website and everything is easy to find," he said. "We should have the same vision for the government."

The ambitions for Americadotgov also go beyond simply helping users find the right information. Coristine said the administration plans to make first-time passport applications fully digital, expanding beyond the online renewal system already available to eligible Americans.

"Specifically with passports, what we’re going to do is we’re gonna make new passports online for the first time ever," Coristine said, describing the existing process as "very manual."

"You have to go in person, you have to get to the post office, you get your photo taken like a CVS or Walgreens," he said.

Under the planned system, Coristine said users would be able to take their passport photo at home, preview how it would appear on the document and complete the process "without leaving the Americadotgov website."

Coristine also offered a glimpse into how President Trump has talked about the broader project, comparing the president’s approach to digital government with his background in hospitality.

"I think the president has been a great host for his entire career. He’s been in the hospitality business, right?" Coristine said. "So any great host knows they have to make things easy, they have to make it all feel clean." @as400495 @DataRepublican
